When someone says they will "move heaven and earth" to do something, it means they will try absolutely everything in their power to make it happen. They will spare no effort, give up no obstacle, and stop at nothing to succeed.

Think of it this way: Heaven and Earth are the two largest things imaginable — the sky above and the ground below. If a person were somehow able to physically move both of them, that would require an almost impossible, superhuman level of effort. So when someone says "I will move heaven and earth," they are using those giant images to express that their effort will be just as extreme and unstoppable.

In short, it means: "I will do everything possible, no matter how hard."
Breaking It Down Word by Word

Even though the phrase sounds literal, it is completely figurative — nobody is actually moving the sky or the ground. This kind of exaggeration used to make a point stronger is called a hyperbole (pronounced hy-PER-boh-lee). It's the same kind of exaggeration you use when you say "I've told you a million times" — you don't mean exactly one million; you just mean "many times."

So in "move heaven and earth," the exaggeration is used to say: "My effort will be so huge, it's like moving the entire universe."

This idiom is very old. A similar expression appeared in the writings of the ancient Greek orator Demosthenes (around 384–322 BC). He used a phrase that meant using every possible force — both the divine (heaven) and the earthly (earth) — to get something done.

The expression later found its way into English literature and everyday speech, and over centuries it became the fixed phrase we know today: "move heaven and earth."

Because it uses "heaven" and "earth," it reflects the old worldview where everything that existed fell into one of two categories: the heavenly realm above, and the earthly world below. Together, they represented everything that exists. So to move both of them means to mobilize everything that exists in service of your goal.
How to Use It — Grammar and Structure

This idiom almost always follows a specific pattern:

[Subject] + will/would + move heaven and earth + to + [achieve something]

Here are some examples:

  • "She will move heaven and earth to make sure her son gets the best medical treatment."
  • "He moved heaven and earth to get the project completed before the deadline."
  • "I would move heaven and earth to protect my family."
  • "The rescue team moved heaven and earth to find the missing hikers."

Notice that it works in different tenses — you can say will move (future), moved (past), or would move (conditional). The core phrase "move heaven and earth" stays the same.
What Kind of Situations Is It Used For?

This idiom is used when the goal being pursued is genuinely important — something the person cares deeply about. You would not normally say "I'll move heaven and earth to find my missing pen," because that's too small and trivial. The idiom carries weight, so it fits situations like:

  • Protecting a loved one
  • Fighting for justice
  • Achieving a lifelong dream
  • Solving a serious crisis
  • Getting someone the help they desperately need

Using it for a very minor goal would sound strange or even funny.
The Feeling Behind It — Tone and Emotion

This idiom carries a tone of deep commitment, fierce determination, and emotional intensity. When a person says it, they want you to feel the full force of their dedication. It's a strong, passionate statement — not casual.

You can use it:

  • About yourself: "I will move heaven and earth to give my kids a better life."
  • About someone else: "She moved heaven and earth to clear her brother's name."

It works in both spoken and written English, and fits both formal and informal situations.

To avoid confusion, here is what the idiom does not mean:

  • It does not mean something is impossible — quite the opposite. It means the person is saying they will succeed no matter what.
  • It does not involve anything supernatural or magical. It's purely about human effort and determination.
  • It does not mean a person is being reckless or careless — it just means they are being maximally determined.
Similar Idioms (In Case You Encounter Them)

Other English idioms carry a similar meaning of "doing everything possible":

  • "Leave no stone unturned" — try every possible option
  • "Go to the ends of the earth" — travel anywhere, do anything to achieve a goal
  • "Pull out all the stops" — use every available resource or strategy
  • "Do everything in one's power" — a more literal, less dramatic way to say the same thing
  • "Bend over backwards" — make a very big effort, often for someone else's benefit

All of these express great effort or determination, but "move heaven and earth" is among the most dramatic and emotionally powerful of them all.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

MeaningTo do absolutely everything possible to achieve a goal
TypeIdiom (specifically, a hyperbole)
ToneStrong, determined, emotional
Used forImportant, serious goals — not trivial things
Key grammarSubject + will/would/moved + heaven and earth + to + goal
Example"She will move heaven and earth to find her missing daughter."

The beauty of this idiom is in its imagery. The moment you hear it, you get a vivid mental picture of someone straining to move the sky and the ground — and that image immediately tells you: this person is not giving up, no matter what.
